record.name: Energy forecasts, geography and measurement boundaries
record.shortName: Energy forecasts, geography and measurement boundaries
record.role: Distinguishes estimated electricity use from conditional demand projections.
record.description: Electricity demand reports combine observations, estimates and scenarios. A global all-data-center forecast includes many uses beyond AI, while an AI-focused subset requires its own definition. The IEA’s April 2026 update and LBNL’s June 2026 US report differ in geography, publication timing and methodology. Their totals cannot be added or treated as competing measurements of the same scope. Historical forecast revisions are useful evidence about changing assumptions, but an older projection should not silently replace a newer one. Power is an instantaneous rate; annual energy integrates changing load, including non-IT overhead when the report’s boundary includes it.

record.tradeoff: Broader forecasts help planning but hide local grid and workload constraints; granular estimates need more uncertain input data.
record.whyAI: AI buildout affects electricity systems, but no annual energy total provides a universal conversion into model throughput or capability.

record.scale: Facility phases to region and world; geography schematic
mechanism: Identify the report date, geography and whether AI is the whole scope or a subset.
Separate estimated historical demand from projected future demand.
Check whether the measure includes cooling and other facility loads.
Compare revisions only after aligning definitions and explaining changed assumptions.
Keep local deliverability and useful workload capacity separate from broad annual electricity totals.
record.misconception: A global data-center forecast is not an AI-only measurement, and a 2030 scenario is not observed consumption.

check.question: Why can a US report not be added to a global total?
options: US electricity uses different physical units
The global scope already includes the United States
check.explanation: The geographies overlap, so adding them double-counts the US contribution.

science.title: Energy from average power
science.explanation: Pavg in GW and Δt in hours gives GWh; divide by 1,000 for TWh.
science.assumptions: Average must cover the same interval and boundary; installed or contracted peak power is not Pavg.

record.learningObjective: Read a dated demand forecast without confusing geography, AI scope or power and energy.
record.engineeringExample: Synthetic constant 1 GW load over 8,760 hours uses 8.76 TWh. A 1 GW nameplate facility does not necessarily use that energy because its average operating load can be lower.

claims.title: IEA estimated 2025 electricity demand
claims.statement: IEA’s April 2026 report estimates 485 TWh of worldwide data-center electricity demand in 2025.
claims.scope: All data centers, with AI-focused facilities a subset
claims.limitations: Estimated baseline, not an AI-only meter total or available power capacity.

claims.title: IEA central 2030 projection
claims.statement: IEA’s April 2026 central projection is 950 TWh of worldwide data-center electricity demand in 2030.
claims.scope: Same broad report scope as the separately labeled 2025 baseline
claims.limitations: Conditional projection, not observed consumption; not additive with US-only LBNL estimates.
